blocks.h: Why use the biggest pile and the second biggest only when blocked?
p: Using the most plentiful letter whenever allowed keeps the piles balanced, so the largest pile is less likely to be left over and unusable. When the largest letter would form three in a row, the code spends one of the next biggest letter as a separator and puts the largest back. Stopping when no separator exists leaves the unavoidable leftover.

bullets: Time: O(n) steps, each with O(log 3) heap work.
Space: O(1): a heap of at most 3 entries (plus the output).

1405.takeaway: Greedy with a max-heap: always take the biggest pile unless that makes three equal letters in a row, then insert the second biggest.

p: The counts for the first rows; `n = 2` gives 54:

blocks.h: Why only two kinds of row?
p: Each row has the shape ABC or ABA (no neighbours equal), and by colour symmetry the number of ways to continue depends only on the shape, not on which colours are used. That reduces the 12 possible rows to 2 states with fixed transition counts. The recurrence matches a brute-force count over all 12 rows for n = 1 to 7: True.

1411.takeaway: Row-shape DP: classify rows as ABC or ABA and use fixed transition counts between the two shapes.

head: Code
What it does
When to reach for it
rows: Size of the block of cards LEFT UNTAKEN
Taking k from the ends leaves one contiguous block of n−k cards in the middle
Slide by adding the entering card and subtracting the leaving one
Leaving the smallest middle block maximises what we take

blocks.h: Why look at the middle instead of the ends?
p: Picking k cards from the two ends in any combination (j from the left, k−j from the right) always leaves a contiguous block of n−k cards. Maximising the picked sum equals minimising that block. A sliding window over all n−k+1 positions covers every combination in O(n) instead of trying each split with its own sum.

1423.takeaway: Invert the problem: the cards you leave form a contiguous window of size n − k; find the window with the minimum sum.

rows: Value → how many times it has arrived
FIFO (First In, First Out) queue; `popleft` is O(1)
Drop front values that are no longer unique
Lazy removal: clean up only when the answer is requested
The front is the first unique value

p: A value stops being unique at the moment a duplicate arrives, but it may be anywhere in the queue. Instead of searching for it, we leave it and discard it only if it reaches the front. Since a value never becomes unique again, each queue entry is popped at most once, so `showFirstUnique` is O(1) amortised.

1429.takeaway: Queue plus counts with lazy removal: skip non-unique values only when they reach the front.

blocks.h: Why two deques instead of calling max()/min() on the window?
p: Each element is appended and popped at most once from each deque, so maintaining the window max and min takes O(n) in total.

1438.takeaway: Sliding window with two monotonic deques for the window maximum and minimum; shrink while max − min exceeds the limit.

p: darts `[[-2, 0], [2, 0], [0, 2], [0, -2]]`, `r = 2` → 4. Candidate centres from each pair:

blocks.h: Why only circles through two darts?
p: Take an optimal circle and slide it until two of its covered darts lie on its boundary, without losing any dart. So some optimal board has two darts on its edge; every such circle is one of the two circles of radius r through some pair. Testing those O(n²) circles against all n darts gives O(n³). A single dart (best = 1) covers the case with no pair.

1453.takeaway: Optimal circle can be shifted until two darts are on its edge: test the two radius-r circles through every pair and count points inside.

Floyd–Warshall order: the middle node k is the OUTER loop
After processing k, paths may use intermediate courses 0…k

p: 3 courses, prerequisites `[[0,1],[1,2]]`; rows of the matrix are separated by `/` (row i lists which courses i reaches):

blocks.h: Why must k be the outer loop?
p: If k were inner, the algorithm would add paths through a single intermediate course at most once per pair and miss longer chains. With k outermost, after round k the matrix correctly answers reachability using only intermediates from {0..k}, and the final round covers all courses.

bullets: Time: O(n³) to build, O(1) per query.

1462.takeaway: Transitive closure with Floyd–Warshall: with the middle node as the outer loop, i reaches j if i reaches k and k reaches j.

The function must return a list

blocks.h: What accumulate does with other functions
p: `accumulate(iterable, func)` applies `func` cumulatively, so `accumulate(nums, max)` gives a running maximum and `accumulate(nums, min)` a running minimum. The default function is addition. The result `[1,3,6,10]` here is also the prefix-sum array used for fast range-sum queries: sum(nums[l..r]) = prefix[r] − prefix[l−1].

1480.takeaway: Running sum = prefix sums: itertools.accumulate does it in one line.

p: If `nums[l] + nums[r] ≤ target`, then `nums[l]` as minimum with any element up to index r as maximum also satisfies it (the others are not larger). The elements at positions l+1 … r can each be in or out of the subsequence, giving 2^(r−l) subsequences that start with `nums[l]`. Then l moves on, since all subsequences with minimum `nums[l]` have been counted.

bullets: Time: O(n log n) for sorting.

1498.takeaway: Sort, then two pointers: if min+max ≤ target, all subsets of the elements between contribute 2^(r−l).

What it does
When to reach for it
rows: Length of the current block of 1s ending here
Add the number of all-1 substrings ENDING at this position
Python integers are unbounded, so one final modulo is enough

blocks.h: Why does adding `run` count every substring once?
p: Every all-1 substring has a unique end position. At a position where the current run of 1s has length L, the substrings ending here that are all 1s start at any of the L positions of the run. So each position contributes L, and the sum over positions equals the number of substrings (a run of length L contributes L(L+1)/2 in total, e.g. 3 gives 1+2+3 = 6).

1513.takeaway: For each position add the length of the current run of 1s: those are the all-1 substrings ending there.

Avoids walking back to the parent

blocks.h: Why return a count array instead of a single number?
p: A node needs to know how many of its OWN letter are below it, but the parent needs counts of ITS letter, which can be any letter. Returning all 26 counts lets every ancestor read what it needs. The cost is 26 operations per merge, so O(26·n) overall, which is fine.

bullets: Space: O(26·n) in the worst case for stored arrays along the recursion plus the graph.

1519.takeaway: Post-order DFS (Depth-First Search) returning a 26-letter count array per subtree and merging children into the parent.

p: Tree: 1 with children 3 (children 5, 6), 2, 4 → diameter 3. Post-order:

A longest path has a highest node, where it goes down into at most two different child branches. Taking the two deepest branches at every node and keeping the maximum over all nodes finds the diameter. With binary trees this is `left + right`; for N-ary trees we need the top two among many children.

bullets: Time: O(n) (each node's children are scanned once).

1522.takeaway: Diameter by tree DP: at each node add the two deepest child depths; return the deepest plus one.

head: Code
What it does
When to reach for it
rows: Kruskal's algorithm processes the cheapest edges first
Weight of the minimum spanning tree (MST) without edge i
If it becomes larger (or disconnected), the edge is critical
MST weight when edge i is included first
If it still equals the base weight, some MST uses edge i
A spanning tree has n−1 edges
Otherwise the graph is disconnected: infinite weight

p: n = 5 with edges `[from, to, weight]`; base MST weight = 7. Weights of the MST when edge i is skipped / forced:
Critical: [0, 1]; pseudo-critical: [2, 3, 4, 5].

bullets: Critical: if removing the edge makes the best tree heavier (or impossible), every minimum tree must contain it.
Pseudo-critical: not critical, but forcing it in still reaches the base weight, so some MST contains it (just not all).
Neither: forcing it makes the tree heavier, so no MST uses it.
Time: O(E² α(n)): about two Kruskal runs per edge, with near-constant Union-Find operations.

1489.takeaway: Re-run Kruskal for each edge, once skipping it (critical if the MST gets heavier) and once forcing it (pseudo-critical if the weight stays the same).

head: Code
What it does
When to reach for it
rows: Greedy placement works left to right
Can m balls be placed with every gap ≥ d?
Feasibility test: place a ball whenever the gap from the last ball is at least d
The minimum gap is at least 1 and at most the total span
Needed because the branch `lo = mid` would loop forever with the lower middle
Binary search on the answer: 'can' is true for small d and false for large d

blocks.h: Why binary search on the distance?
p: Feasibility is monotone: if balls fit with minimum gap d, they also fit with any smaller gap. So the largest feasible d can be found by binary search over d, with a greedy O(n) check each time. The greedy check is right because placing each ball as far left as allowed leaves the most room for later balls.

bullets: Time: O(n log n + n log R) where R = max position − min position.

1552.takeaway: Binary search on the answer with a greedy feasibility check: place a ball whenever the gap from the previous one is at least d.

head: Code
What it does
When to reach for it
rows: Room j can only be reached through rooms 0…j−1, so the tallest box that can reach it is limited by the lowest room so far
Match small boxes with small capacities
The smallest unplaced box fits this room

blocks.h: Why does the capacity depend on the minimum so far?
p: Boxes enter from the left, so a box that reaches room j must pass every room before it. If room 1 has height 3, nothing taller than 3 gets beyond it, so rooms behind it have capacity at most 3 even if they are taller. The prefix minimum is exactly that limit.

blocks.h: Why match smallest boxes with smallest capacities?
p: Any placement can be rearranged so that the smallest used boxes go into the smallest rooms without losing boxes. The greedy pointer pass does this in O(n) after sorting, using each room at most once.

bullets: Time: O(n log n + m log m).

1564.takeaway: Prefix minimum gives each room's effective height; sort rooms and boxes and match greedily.

blocks.h: Why swap so that we loop over the smaller dict?
p: The work is the number of lookups, equal to the size of the dictionary we iterate over. Iterating over the smaller one makes the cost O(min(a, b)) instead of O(a). Only index 3 is shared here: 2 × 4 = 8.

bullets: Time: Constructor O(n); dot product O(min(non-zeros of the two vectors)).

1570.takeaway: Store a sparse vector as a dict of its non-zeros and multiply only the indexes present in both, iterating over the smaller one.
